newsitem.title: USA: Compaq strategy to fuel lower PC prices.
newsitem.headline: Compaq strategy to fuel lower PC prices.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp is embarking on a another major re-engineering of its business that its executives said will lead to lower PC prices, higher profit margins and even more market share.
The moves are part of the Houston-based company's quest to eventually become one of the world's top three computer vendors.

This summer, the world's largest PC manufacturer will introduce its first PC products to implement its new build-to-order and build-to-configure manufacturing strategy. Under this strategy, Compaq will build its computers as they are ordered by customers, instead of manufacturing in advance based on forecasts.

In interviews here, Compaq executives here said this re-engineering of its business was more important than its 1992 launch of lower-cost PCs, a move that reverberated throughout the PC industry and helped Compaq leapfrog International Business Machines Corp. as the No. 1 maker of PCs.
"It is much more important to us than what we did in 1992," said Earl Mason, Compaq's chief financial officer. "It will significantly grow our market share and our profits."

Mason declined to specify how much the move to revamp and lower its manufacturing costs would boost future profits, but he said that it would begin to take effect in the third quarter and be fully in place by year-end.

Mason said the new manufacturing strategy -- where its resellers and distributors will only carry a maximum of two weeks inventory instead of five weeks -- Compaq will have the most competitively priced products in the industry, as it addresses competition from direct marketers Dell Computer Corp. and Gateway 2000 Inc.
Compaq said it will be able to offer products at 10 percent to 20 percent lower than current prices.

"There is no question that it will lower prices," said Jim Schraith, Compaq vice president and general manager for North America. "We will become much more competitive and in some categories the price leader."
Schraith also said he expected Compaq's competition to re-examine how they work with the companies that resell and distribute their products.
Currently, Compaq ships a certain number of PCs to its distributors and resellers in configurations that it believes the market wants.

Then, these resellers, based on orders from customers, sometimes have to add new parts or reconfigure the boxes themselves -- for example, swapping a one gigabyte hard disk drive for a two gigabyte drive, or more memory chips. This second reconfiguration adds extra costs to the product.
Another example is when Compaq ships a certain number of PCs with Pentium chips at speeds of 160 megahertz, and the model that becomes more popular is the 200 megahertz.

Now, when a product isn't selling to forecast, Compaq cuts prices to help move the inventory, but it also has to pay its resellers and dealers for price protection, because they have already purchased the products from Compaq to be sold at the higher prices.
With fewer weeks on inventory on hand, Compaq's price protection payments will decline.
Both Compaq and its resellers will also be able to take advantage of the fluctuations in component prices, such as the lower costs in microprocessors.
